image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Bubble chart / proportional symbol chart over body silhouettes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- **Small multiples / faceting by sport**: six side-by-side panels (Football, Hockey, Wrestling, Lacrosse, Soccer, Basketball).  
- Within each panel, bubbles are positioned anatomically on a body outline.  
- No stacking.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate side-by-side panels; panel title |
| Body part / injury location (Head, Shoulder, Arm, Hand, Trunk, Thigh, Knee, Lower leg, Ankle) | Categorical/nominal | Spatial position on body silhouette; text labels |
| Injuries per 10,000 competition plays | Quantitative | Bubble/circle size (area); numeric label inside each bubble |

If useful, the body silhouette acts as a background reference for position, not as a separate data variable.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that head injuries are the most common type of injury in each sport. This makes me wonder about the type of head protection each sport requires and the equipment’s effectiveness. I also noticed that football generally has the most of every kind of injury. At the very least, the number of each injury is on the higher end of the range. This is surprising to me because football players are required to wear the most gear out of all the sports listed in this graph. Since football players wear helmets and padding I would expect them to receive fewer injuries than basketball, who have no protective gear. This data is very telling of how dangerous these five sports can be with the current rules of each game and the protective equipment required. These two things should be reassessed two bring down the number of injuries in the future. For each sport, protective gear should be added or improved in the places where boys received a large number of injuries, such as the ankle for basketball and the shoulder for hockey. A catchy headline for this graph would be Hitting Points on High School Boys Sports Injuries.

comments.raw_comment: What I noticed was how head injuries were the ones that brought the reader's attention and from general knowledge, we know that a head injury, or maybe brain injury, is one of the more serious types of injuries out there. Therefore, choosing to focus their attention on head injuries shows the desperate cry for awareness to be spread about how serious these injuries can be. I also noticed that the more physical contact sports tend to have to most injury, like football, with players hitting each other all the time to prevent the other team to make a point. While in basketball there’s little to no contact and the players seem to be choosing a less dangerous sport. I noticed that wrestling, lacrosse, and soccer all had similar injuries, which is interesting because wrestling is a very intense sport where members are the team are actively fighting other people, while lacrosse and soccer are both field sports. What I wonder is if the numbers inside the bubbles are how many times members of the teams were injured and if how many members were there would affect the results of the graph. I believe that this affects the community because it brings awareness to danger in sports, regardless of being a low-impact sport or a very heavily physical sport, it shows how injuries can happen. A catchy headline could be: “Brain vs. Game.”

I could never imagine playing a sport that involved a huge chance of being severely hurt. If I had kids, I would never want them doing a sport where high risk of injury was a part of the game. Damage to someone’s brain is nothing to take lightly, and football is the number one contender, by far. 

Ankle, knee and hand injuries also occur in football players much more than any other sport. But truly, these seem insignificant compared to irreversible head injuries. Your hand can heal and your ankle can get wrapped in a cast, but you only get one brain and its healing process is very different than other body parts. 

I hope football players and coaches start to realize the danger and long term effects of damaging teen’s bodies like that.

Lacrosse has more knee injuries than Hockey, but Hockey is still placed higher on the leaderboard for the most injuries. Every sport instead of football has 2 trunk injuries for every 10,000 competition plays. Wrestling has the least amount of thigh injuries, which surprised me. I noticed that head injuries were the most common. Lastly, soccer and lacrosse have the same amount of head injuries.

I wonder how hockey and football have more injuries than wrestling. I do because you don't wear any protective gear in wrestling, whereas in hockey and football, you wear tons of pads and gear. Also, I wonder why hockey has more shoulder injuries than football, because in football, you mainly use your shoulder to tackle. Lastly, why does wrestling have less hand injuries than football, because in wrestling you are constantly grabbing things for the whole match.

comments.raw_comment:
“Hard hitters"
The first thing I noticed about this graph is that football, hockey, and wrestling all have the most injuries, which was expected. But why so many head injuries, and why are there any in the first place? The head is easily the worst place to be damaged, as it can lead to concussions and other issues in the future. I think the coaches need to realize that the boys on the team are still kids, and need to play in safer conditions with more protective gear. 
I also wonder why football was the most dangerous sport when you would expect hockey and wrestling to be the same, or even worse. A reason for this may be that football is just too aggressive, and I think they should cut back on the amount of rough contact they make with each other.

comments.raw_comment: The infographic illustrates the variation in the injuries students sustain across different sports. The author used different sized circles overlayed on top of specific body areas to highlight the number of specific injuries for a particular sport in a sample of 10,000 students. We can conclude from the infographic that football is associated with more frequent injuries, especially head, hand, knee, and angle injuries. These results are not surprising – football is contact-heavy, and involves collission of heads, pushing, and quick changes of directions, all which correspond to higher rates of injuries. While the results make sense, I am extremely curious on how the 10,000 samples were collected. The region and district in which a student plays is extremely important because different areas have different regulations on contact and perhaps normalize certain forms of contact that other regions do not. Furthermore, blocking between experienced athletes and new athletes would be effective in order to see if there are any differences between the two groups, as new athletes are likely less fit and have higher risks of becoming injured. Regardless, the infographic and study conducted are important in understanding the relationship between high school sports and injuries – it can be used in helping guide parents in what sports their child should play, and in regulating policies of specific sports. I would title it "When Recreation Becomes Injurious."

Every athlete will get injured at some point, it’s a part of the sport. But just because injuries are common, and expected doesn’t mean they aren’t causing some serious damage. 

I noticed that head injuries in football are almost double in any other sport, but with it being America’s most popular sport I wonder why there aren’t more people working to make it safer for those playing it.The short term effects of a concussion are bad enough for high school students, who are too busy to be basically useless for a week or two at school while they’re recovering. That time can set you back! But from what we know, too many head injuries can cause serious effects later in life. Playing football in high school shouldn't mean they should be punished with early memory loss!

I think this would have shown the difference in the roughness you usually see in boys playing sports. I know a lot of injuries when a boy plays a game than if a girl plays the same competition.

comments.raw_comment:
The Wellbeing of Student Athletes
I am a student athlete. I run cross country and track year round, which may not seem like a high impact sport, but it produces many injuries. I know this because I had a stress fracture for almost a year and many of my teammates, both male and female, struggle with the frustration and pain of injuries as well. From my experience, I wonder about the psychological effect on students from being sidelined during their injury and how it varies by sport. I also wonder how the injuries within sports occur. In sports such as football and hockey that are known for high physical impact, it is heavily implied that injuries are caused by the impact. In other sports such as soccer or basketball where there is less contact, I begin to question if the injuries are from overuse (which is what my personal injury was from) or from the contact within the sport. By questioning this, I began to notice how common injuries are for athletes, despite the use of protection such as helmets, shin guards, etc. If injuries are both physically and psychologically taxing for students, who are still adolescents, we should be making sure we are taking all preventative measures possible to ensure that minimal student injuries occur.

Thanks to all who responded. We had catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs, including “Athletes In Danger!” by Brianna of Hancock, Maryland, and “Use Your Head.  Are These Sports Safe?” by Devyn of Academy of St. Elizabeth, Morristown, New Jersey. Some plays on words like, "Friday Night Hospital Lights" by Mairead of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, NC. You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage. Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.

The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, whose sports injuries are not in these infographics since these are only for high school boys, and Corey Andreasen of Leiden, The Netherlands, who is well represented in this graph.

Headline: Why so many injuries?
   There are far too many injuries during high school men's sports, especially head injuries. This is what I noticed while observing a graph about how often high school sports players are injured while playing a sport. As a high school lacrosse player, I am appalled by the number of total injuries that occurred. During just 10,000 competition plays, 37 marked injuries took place. I was shocked that there were this many. Even though I know that the sport is very contact-focused, I did not expect a number that high. This number, while it is shocking, is only fourth-highest among popular sports, and it pales in comparison to the number that occur in football. Football causes 34 head injuries every 10,000 plays. That is almost the total number of all that occurred during lacrosse, and that number is only referring to head injuries. In addition, this number only encompasses competition plays, when practice time is much more common than competition and provides even more opportunities for injury. These games need to be safer.
    With this in mind, I wonder what the effect of safer game rules and better equipment would be on the amount of injuries in these sports. If there were better padding in sports with too many injuries, such as football, perhaps there would be less bodily harm. Better helmets could lower the amount of head injuries, and perhaps new rules could make the game less violent in order to make high school sports safer for the youth.

comments.raw_comment:
The Top Sport of America… Football
Ever since middle school I have noticed that football has the most injuries overall, despite that football is still one of the top sports in America and is enjoyed by the viewers and the players. When I was younger I wanted to play football but my parents always said no, I never understood that until now. They were concerned for my well being and scared that the injuries would have an affect on my school work and my life and looking back now I understand their worries. I have a number of friends who have played football  and have gotten injuries from knee injuries all the way to a severe concussions. Injuries to the head cause a number of problems such as having issues focusing in school and  in life in general which will affect their future selves and how they can provide for their families. Through all of the effort in making football a safer sport there are still too many injuries. I wonder what the NFL’s next step towards safety in football will be.

As this does make sense because it is arguably the most contact sport out of the list, it still is ridiculous how many injuries there are. I wonder what we could do to make all of these sports safer without taking away the fun aspects of it. Head injuries alone should be our number one concern. You could be a soccer player for high school, make it into college, and then one injury could leave you never being able to play again. With this being said, I would try to come up with ideas to make these sports safer to play while still being able to have a good time.

comments.raw_comment:
"How Many Injuries Will It Take"
How many students have to get injured in order to start taking measures to try and prevent these injuries? When looking at this graph I notice how clear it is that football has an insanely high amount of head injuries. This is unsettling to see because my brother plays football and he's only in middle school. When I was at one of his games, I witnessed a kid on the other team sprain his neck. It was really scary. The ambulance came and he was in the hospital for 2 days. The injuries start even earlier than high school. This many head injuries while their brains are still developing could be dangerous. I definitely don't play football but I myself have had a head injury once before and just that one was enough for me to feel dizzy and have a headache if I read for too long. 
I wonder if there has been any progress in trying to prevent even more head injuries from happening. I find it interesting that basketball has the least amount of injuries even though there seems to be at least one injury during every game.

  I notice in the graphs that every sport has it's injuries but one injury they all have in common is the head injury. Why the head? I understand people having their own loves for activities they enjoy just like I do but why not spend more time having fun doing those activities than worrying about that next scholarship or if you're going to get injured or impressing someone else? Why not just do it for you?

It is more common for long time football players to suffer from problems such as brain damage. This graph definitely shows that football deals with the most head injuries so this makes me think about long term issues.

Headline: "Friday Night Hospital Lights"

When I studied the graph for the first time, I noticed that the most popular American sport, football, has the highest number of injuries sustained per 10,000 competition plays, specifically head injuries.  I knew that football, hockey, and wrestling would have the most injuries even before I read this article due to my prior knowledge.  I have seen many of the Varsity football players at my school in casts and braces for several weeks, but then right back on the field when their doctors said they could, which can cause permanent damage to their bodies.  Also, one of my friends is on the wrestling team and she seriously injured her knee at a match and might not be able to wrestle for the rest of the season.  

I wonder where this data was collected from, whether it all came from one region of the country or from all over.  I wonder this because I have family in Northern Minnesota, and hockey is the most popular sport there by far.  On the other hand, here in North Carolina, hockey isn't very popular at all, but lacrosse is.  If this data is only collected from a certain region of the country, I wonder how much it would differ if it was collected from other regions as well.

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: Hungry to Win, How Hungry is Too Hungry?
From this graph I notice that there are many risks associated with playing any sport, especially as a boy, due to their competitive and aggressive nature. Football is most commonly known for its head injuries, the debates on how to make it safer are plentiful. Constant arguing over whether or not to change the rules, the equipment, or even the entire sport to make it safer for kids. Something that needs to be pointed out is that there is risk associated with everything sport you play, it just depends on how comfortable you are with taking those risks. After looking at this graph, I wonder what keeps these boys interested in these sports if there is such a high risk of injury. I guess it could be their high adrenaline levels, their aggressive nature as stated before, or just their hunger to the best. But where is the line between risk and reward? All Injuries add up over time and take a large toll on your body? As an athlete, I’m not against playing sports and getting hurt, it builds character and helps us develop into stronger people, but it’s the ones who push themselves past their threshold that I'm worried about. Sports are good for your health, mentally and physically, for the most part, it’s one of the best ways to release your anger and frustration, and it keeps you in shape but you need to understand when you've overworked yourself.

comments.raw_comment:
Heading: Friday Night Fatalities 
If you take time to study the graph you easily notice the fact the football has the most substantial injuries. The first three don’t surprise me because they are contact sports. What does surprise me is the fact that football has an overwhelming amount of injuries. The worst part is the fact that the head injuries are so high. Football players wear a good amount of protection yet they still rank the highest for injuries. This leads me to ask the question, how protected are they actually. One of my friends from middle school had suffered about three concussions from his time while playing football. He was a quarterback with a lot of potential, but was taken off the team by his mother out of fear, and rightfully so. Before this school year started my friend was debating weather to play football or wrestling. I was relieved to hear he would be joining the wrestling team. I wondered why I was so relieved by what he told me. Then I came to the conclusion that you hear more horror stories about football and all the awful articles about brain injuries and their consequences. I wonder what we can do to make these sports a bit more safer all together.
